name: Olga Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining me, Olga. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no links to companies, unions, parties or government. Nothing you say will be traced back to you. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a buyer at Norvale Components. We distribute electronic parts, so I buy connectors, cables, power supplies and small chips from factories in Asia and Europe, and sell them on to companies that build machines and medical kit. A normal day is checking lead times, which is how many weeks a factory needs to make something, and moving orders around so nobody's production line stops. I've got an AI assistant open all day that reads supplier emails and flags anything late.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what drains you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's a puzzle with real stakes. If I miss a connector, a customer can't finish a ventilator. What drains me is time zones, calls at seven in the morning with Shenzhen and at six in the evening with a plant in Ohio. My boyfriend Daniel says I talk about lead times in my sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That's not what I see day to day, but fine, let's say it stalls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the tools are still useful, they just didn't become magic. To friends I'd say I'm glad the AI reads my inbox and I still get paid. Online I'd probably post a little thread about what actually worked and what didn't, because people love that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's fine. My job stays, my pay's good for a buyer, and I've got savings plus some shares. I'd be a bit disappointed, because I like being early on things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the email assistant and build a better lead-time tracker with it. I'd keep putting money into my index fund every month like I do now. Maybe I'd go for the senior buyer job when Ines retires next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would bother you even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Supply shocks, always. When a factory floods or a port shuts, my week as a buyer falls apart, AI or not. That's what keeps buyers busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the senior buyer job mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More money, and running the team's supplier list instead of my own share of it. I'd want to show I can do it with fewer late orders. If AI stalls, the promotion becomes my big thing for next year.

say: I'd say the tools stayed **useful** but didn't become magic.
I'd post a short thread on **what actually worked** and what didn't.
think: My job stays, with **good pay**, savings and some shares.
I'd be a bit **disappointed**, because I like being early on things.
do: Build a better **lead-time tracker** with the email assistant.
Keep paying into my **index fund** every month.
Apply for the **senior buyer** job when Ines retires.
S0.quote: When a factory floods or a port shuts, my week as a buyer falls apart, AI or not.
fieldNote: Olga is **comfortable with AI** and treats a stall as mildly disappointing.
Her real work risk is **supply shocks**, like floods and port closures.
She is focused on a **promotion** when a senior colleague retires.

steps.text: Build a lead-time tracker using the email assistant
Keep the monthly payment into the index fund
Apply for the senior buyer job when Ines retires

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's basically what's happening already at Norvale, just faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say this is our chance to stop firefighting and plan properly. To friends I'd say buyers who use the AI tools will be fine and buyers who don't will struggle, which is blunt but true. Online I'd share what I'm building, because it helps people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I come out of it well. I'm already the one who sets up the tools, so I'd likely run the buying system rather than be replaced by it. The team might shrink from eight to five over a few years, and I'd feel bad for some of them, but it wouldn't be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd ask to lead the rollout of the new buying software and write the rules it follows. I'd do a short online course in supply chain data, around six hundred. And I'd ask for a pay rise tied to it, because if the team shrinks, the ones left are doing more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited. I'd sleep fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said some colleagues would struggle. Who do you have in mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marek, mostly. He's been here fifteen years, knows every factory manager in Taiwan, but he won't touch the tools. I'd try to pair him with the system, so his contacts and the AI work together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Daniel? Does this picture touch his work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daniel tests software, so yes, a lot of testing would go to AI. He's more nervous than me. In this picture he'd probably have to move into setting up the testing tools, which he could do.

say: I'd tell colleagues it's a chance to **stop firefighting** and plan.
I'd say buyers who **use the tools** will be fine, which is blunt but true.
think: I'd likely **run the buying system** rather than be replaced by it.
The team might shrink **from eight to five**, but not me.
do: Ask to lead the **software rollout** and write its rules.
Take a **six-hundred** online course in supply chain data.
Ask for a **pay rise** tied to the bigger workload.
S1.quote: Buyers who use the AI tools will be fine and buyers who don't will struggle, which is blunt but true.
fieldNote: Olga expects to **gain**, not lose, as the person who sets up the tools.
She shows care for **Marek** and wants to pair his contacts with the system.
Her partner's **software testing** job adds a second exposure to the household.

steps.text: Lead the rollout of Norvale's new buying software
Take an online course in supply chain data this year
Ask for a pay rise tied to the larger workload

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay. That's me and Daniel both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say let's get real about what the company still needs people for, and quickly. To friends I'd say the people who thought they were safe because they were good with AI, like me, aren't safe either. I'd probably stop posting, it would feel like bragging about a sinking ship.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, if AI can do any thinking work, it can do mine, and it can do Daniel's. That's both incomes going within two years. We've got savings and my shares, maybe a year and a half of rent and food together, but it'd be the first time I didn't feel ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd move most of the shares into cash, because markets would go mad. We'd cut out the trips and the takeaways and look at a cheaper flat when the lease ends in June. I'd look at roles on the supplier side, like going to factories to check quality, because that's physical and robots don't do it till 2031. And I'd start selling refurbished test equipment online, which I know how to source.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's the both-of-us part. I'd be lying awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. Does that help you here at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It helps me see it coming, that's all. Being good at the AI tool doesn't matter when the tool doesn't need you. It's a strange feeling, being early and still being caught.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum, honestly. She moved countries at thirty with two suitcases and started over. She'd say we've done hard things before. Then she'd ask if we're eating properly.

say: I'd urge the firm to decide what it **needs people** for, fast.
I'd say people **good with AI**, like me, aren't safe either.
think: Both **our incomes** go within two years, mine and Daniel's.
Savings and shares cover about **eighteen months**, but I wouldn't feel ahead.
do: Move most **shares into cash** before markets swing.
Cut trips and takeaways and find a **cheaper flat** in June.
Seek **factory quality** roles and sell refurbished test kit online.
feel: **Alarmed**, lying awake doing **sums** because it's both of us.
S2.quote: Being good at the AI tool doesn't matter when the tool doesn't need you.
fieldNote: Olga's alarm comes from the **household**, since her partner's job is exposed too.
Being an early adopter gives her **foresight but no protection**.
She moves fast: **cash, cheaper flat**, hands-on quality work, a side business.

steps.text: Move most of the share portfolio into cash this month
Move to a cheaper flat when the lease ends in June
Apply for factory quality inspector roles with component makers
Sell refurbished electronic test equipment online

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. 2031 and 2034. That changes things a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say five years is enough time to rebuild how we work, so let's plan instead of panicking. To friends I'd say get your skills and money sorted by 2030. I'd post about it, carefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I still think my buying job goes in 2031. But five years is enough for me to have a second thing going, and for Daniel too. I'd be thirty-two, which is a good age to change direction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd keep doing the job well and save harder, maybe a third of my pay. I'd start the refurbished test equipment business properly, with a small website, and see if it can make a few hundred a month. I'd look at a part-time engineering certificate, because people who can open a machine and fix it get until 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked. I'd have a plan, but it's still my whole career changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the side business really last past AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not forever, AI will run online shops too. But buying and testing actual machines is hands-on, and that's where the extra three years are. A side business selling test equipment is a bridge, not a pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Daniel do with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's talked about becoming a teacher, maths or computing. Kids still need a person in front of them. I'd tell him to start the teaching course in year two, so he's qualified before 2031.

say: I'd say five years is enough to **rebuild how we work**.
I'd tell friends to get **skills and money** sorted by 2030.
think: Five years lets me and Daniel build **a second thing** each.
do: Save **a third** of my pay while doing the job well.
Launch the **test equipment** business with a small website.
Take a part-time **engineering certificate** for hands-on repair work.
feel: **Anxious** but not panicked, because I'd **have a plan**.
S3.quote: A side business selling test equipment is a bridge, not a pension.
fieldNote: Olga uses the **three-year robot gap** to aim at hands-on repair skills.
She plans for **both earners**, nudging Daniel toward teaching.
She is honest that her side business is **temporary**.

steps.text: Save a third of each paycheck from now until 2030
Launch a small website for refurbished test equipment
Start a part-time engineering certificate in electronics repair

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. 2036 and 2039. Okay, that feels manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say this is the version where we have no excuses. To friends I'd say it's like knowing about a pension crash ten years ahead. Online I'd share the plan I make, because ten years of planning in public helps people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is enough to change career properly, maybe twice. I'd be thirty-seven when buying ends. By then I'd want to own something, like a share in a repair business or a property that pays rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep buying and keep using the tools, and probably go for the senior role. I'd put more into investments over the first few years, then move toward property around year five. And I'd do the engineering certificate slowly, one module a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I'd say. Not scared, just aware.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd want to own something. Why ownership?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because when AI does the work, the people who own the machines and buildings still get paid. I'm not rich, but with ten years I can own a small piece. That's the pragmatic answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would it change plans with Daniel, like a home or family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably still buy a place in the next few years and maybe have kids around thirty-one. Ten years is long enough to plan normally. Two years and I'd hold everything.

say: I'd say this version leaves **no excuses**.
I'd compare it to knowing about a **pension crash** ten years ahead.
think: Ten years is enough to **change career** properly, maybe twice.
By thirty-seven I'd want to **own something**, like property or a repair business.
do: Keep buying and go for the **senior role**.
Invest more now and move toward **property** around year five.
Take the **engineering certificate** one module a year.

fieldNote: Olga's long-term answer is **ownership**: property, shares or a business.
She keeps **normal family plans** with ten years, but would pause them at two.
Her centre outlook shows as **pragmatism**, not blame.

steps.text: Go for the senior buyer role at Norvale

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it hits me and Daniel at once. What would help is time, really, even six months' notice from employers, and some kind of income support while people retrain, so a couple like us doesn't burn all its savings in one go.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether being early helps. Everyone tells you to learn AI and you'll be fine, and in the fast version learning AI just means I see the wave first. I did learn it, and it doesn't save me.

headlineQuote: Everyone tells you to learn AI and you'll be fine, and in the fast version learning AI just means I see the wave first.
portrait: Olga is a **27-year-old electronics buyer** who uses AI every day and likes being early.
She has **savings and shares**, and a partner whose software testing job is also exposed.
She is calm in slower scenarios, expecting to **run the tools** rather than be replaced.
In AGI by 2028 she becomes **alarmed**, because both household incomes go at once.
With more time she aims at **hands-on repair** skills and owning property or a business.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it would hit her and Daniel at once.
whatWouldHelp: Notice from employers and **income support** while people retrain.
